source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: People retrieve stories that share objects and surface detail far more than stories that share only causal structure. The same people rate the structural matches as the most sound. Retrievability and soundness are uncorrelated.
numbers: Exp 2 (36 undergrads, one week delay): proportion reminded 0.56 literal similarity, 0.53 surface match, 0.12 analogy (structure only), 0.09 first-order-relations-only match. Soundness vs reminding r(52)=.15, ns. Exp 1: 30 MIT students.
quote: Analogical matches were rated as sound but were not well retrieved, and the opposite was true for surface matches.
limits: Cued recall of read stories after a delay; in-lab stories, not real problems. Soundness ratings came from separate raters.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent retrieve by 'which stored case looks closest'. Looks-closest and is-useful are different axes, and the first is what unaided memory serves.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness (Exp 3 and Exp 4)
finding: Exp 3 asked what drives the surface advantage: object-only matches (same objects, almost no shared relations) were not recalled as well as surface matches that also kept first-order relations. So surface plus some shared relations is the strong cue, not bare object overlap. Exp 4 shows the structure was stored: the failure is at retrieval, not encoding.
numbers: Exp 4 (27 undergrads, forced-choice recognition after one week): group given surface-similar probes chose the literal match 82% of the time (16.46/20, chi2=61, p<.0001); group given structure-only probes chose the analogy only 55% (11/20), at chance.
quote: We conclude that the locus of the surface superiority effect is at retrieval.
limits: Recognition is easier than recall; 'stored but not retrieved' relies on both groups having encoded alike.
agent_relevance: Relational structure can sit in memory and still be unreachable from a probe that lacks surface overlap. The fix is to change the probe (re-describe it), not to enlarge memory.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness (MAC/FAC simulation section)
finding: A two-stage model reproduces the human ordering. MAC is a cheap dot product over content vectors of predicates. FAC then runs full structure mapping on the few MAC survivors. The human retrievability order LS > SS > AN >= FOR came out in the simulation too.
numbers: Simulation on 9 story sets (36 stories): mean items MAC produced 3.3, FAC accepted 1.5. With distractors, base story passed both stages 1.0 for literal, .89 for surface, .67 for analogy probes.
limits: Hand-coded predicate representations of only 9 of 20 story sets; ordinal match only, not a fit to human proportions.
agent_relevance: Cheap wide recall followed by an expensive structural filter is a design we can copy: embedding or keyword recall of N candidates, then a structural comparison step run by code or a model.

source: Law, Forbus, Gentner (1994) Simulating similarity-based retrieval: a comparison of ARCS and MAC/FAC
finding: A rival model of retrieval (ARCS, a connectionist network using semantic similarity) was tested against MAC/FAC on the same representations. Both retrieve a fable (Sour Grapes) from variants. ARCS was distracted when 25 plays were added to memory and seemed to prefer larger descriptions. MAC/FAC results did not change.
numbers: MAC/FAC about two orders of magnitude faster than ARCS on identical data. Memory: 100 fables, later plus 25 plays (125 items).
quote: In retrieval, the special demands of large memories argue for simpler algorithms; the cost of false positives is much higher.
limits: Simulation paper by the MAC/FAC authors, small memories. The PDF text is poor OCR so figures were read from running text only.
agent_relevance: Retrieval cost and false positives grow with memory size. The authors note retrieval is iterative in practice: a missed match can be caught after the probe is re-represented, so false negatives are cheaper than false positives.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson, Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events
finding: Comparing two analogous cases at learning time makes people better at retrieving good structural matches from their own long-term memory, and at transferring. Experiment 1 used professional management consultants and real memories.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=124 consultants; 64 comparison, 60 separate): retrieval rating 1.25 vs 0.82 on a 0-2 scale, t(122)=2.65, p<.01; case description quality 1.45 vs 0.98, t(122)=2.97; contingent agreements in role play 59% vs 33%, chi2(1,N=62)=4.22. 88% of comparers linked the two cases vs 17% of separate-case readers. Exp 2 (accounting masters students, N=36): retrieval 1.47 vs 0.59, t(34)=2.88, p<.01.
quote: Comparing two analogous examples at recall time promotes retrieving analogical matches stored in memory.
limits: Coder ratings on a 0-2 scale; retrievals are self-reported memories; correlation of schema quality with retrieval varied across studies (rs=.18, .31, .36, .51). One explicit retrieval prompt, not spontaneous use on a real task.
agent_relevance: Strongest human evidence that abstraction made at storage or probe time fixes access. For the agent: when two solved cases exist, force a compare-and-write-the-principle step and index by that principle.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson, Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events (Experiments 3 to 5)
finding: Control conditions show the effect needs a real comparison, not just two cases read: both the separate-case and single-case controls did worse. In a controlled memory set, comparers recalled the structural match more and the surface-similar lure less. With the radiation problem and a delay, comparing two current problems raised solving.
numbers: Exp 3 (3 conditions, about 50 participants): retrieval F(1,48)=10.38, p<.005; comparison beat separate and single-case (Dunnett p<.05). Exp 4 (N=73): recalled the prior analogous example 27% comparison vs 6% separate, chi2=6.12; retrieved a surface-similar lure 30% vs 78%. Exp 5 (N=227, filled delay): tumor problem solved 31% vs 5%, chi2(1)=24.71, p<.001; Red Adair problem 41% vs 30%, chi2=2.89, p=.08 (not significant). Exp 3 trade-off principle case-description effect p=.10.
quote: Fewer comparison participants (30%) retrieved a surface similar example than separate-case participants (78%).
limits: The effect was not uniform: on one problem pair the trend was not significant because the separate group did unusually well.
agent_relevance: The lure rate drops from 78% to 30% while the structural rate rises, so comparison changes what is retrieved, not only how much. Boundary: gain depends on the problem pair, so test per task.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson, Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events (simulations 1 to 4 with MAC/FAC and SME)
finding: The mechanism was checked in simulation. A relational schema built by SME from two cases, used as a probe, retrieved analogical matches; a single story probe retrieved shallow matches. Schemas hold a larger share of relational predicates than the base stories.
numbers: Single base-story probes: shallow match returned 86% and 100% (two stories), analogical match 14% and 0%. Schema probes: analogical retrievals 86%, shallow 29%, first-order 14%. Relational predicates in schemas about 80% vs 40% in base stories. When literal-similarity items were added to memory they dominated retrieval (100%).
limits: Small hand-built memories; shows plausibility, not proof that people do this.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete recipe: compare two cases, keep only the shared relational skeleton, use it as the query. Literal near-copies in memory will still crowd out everything else.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson, Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge: analogical abstraction supports relational retrieval of past events (discussion: baseline retrieval is poor)
finding: Poor relational retrieval without comparison is robust, and here it held for motivated professionals who knew a relevant case from their own work. Many retrieved a partial structural match. Some preferred writing nothing over a clearly poor match.
numbers: Exp 1 retrieval types (literal / analogy / shallow / none): separate-case 5% / 42% / 40% / 13% (N=60); comparison 8% / 63% / 20% / 9% (N=64); overall 6% / 52% / 30% / 11%.
limits: Self-report memory task with explicit retrieval instructions, so it measures retrieval on request, not spontaneous reminding.
agent_relevance: Even when told to look for the relation, unaided retrieval returns half-matches. A reject output ('nothing found') is a feature, not a failure.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams: comparing cases promotes learning and transfer
finding: Teams that compared two training cases were more likely to use a value-adding contingent contract in a new face-to-face negotiation that shared no surface features with the cases. Comparison helped over no training; separate-case study did not.
numbers: Contingent contract formed: compare 24/60 (40%) vs separate 8/37 (22%), chi2(1,N=97)=3.50, p=.06 (marginal). Comparison vs no-training baseline chi2(N=83)=4.95, p<.05; separate vs baseline chi2(N=60) ns. Joint gains $4.76M vs $4.28M vs $4.19M baseline. All comparers described links between the cases, 18% of separate-case participants did. Intact teams vs solo negotiators not reliably different (32% intact).
limits: The headline contrast with separate cases is only marginal (p=.06); team vs individual made no reliable difference.
agent_relevance: Training by comparing worked cases pays even when the target shares nothing superficial with them. Use a prior near 18 percentage points, not a large effect.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach, Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review (abstract page)
finding: Across 57 experiments (336 tests), case comparison beat sequential, single-case or non-analogous study, traditional instruction and controls. Four of 15 moderators mattered: objective of the comparison, whether a principle was given, content, and lag to test.
numbers: Average d = 0.50, 95% CI [0.44, 0.56]. Stronger when learners are asked to find similarities, when the principle is given after the comparison, with perceptual content, and with immediate testing.
quote: Greater learning was associated with asking learners to find similarities between cases, providing principles after comparisons.
limits: Only the abstract was read (full PDF link returned 404). Outcomes are learning and transfer tests, not spontaneous retrieval. Immediate testing was favoured, so delay probably shrinks the benefit.
agent_relevance: Medium effect, moderated. Order matters: compare first, then supply the principle. Write the abstraction into the library right away.

source: Alfieri et al. (2013) lag subgroup (search snippet)
finding: For studies where the principle came after comparison, a search snippet reports immediate testing d=1.07 and testing on later days d=1.60, difference not significant.
numbers: N=29 conditions, Q(1)=3.67, p=.056.
limits: Snippet only, not checked in the paper. It appears to run against the abstract's 'test immediately' finding, so treat as unresolved.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the benefit decays; the two sources disagree, so measure retention in our own tests.

source: Pedone, Hummel, Holyoak (2001) The use of diagrams in analogical problem solving
finding: Static diagrams used as the source for the radiation problem were not accessed spontaneously (baseline-like rate) but worked after a hint. Animating the diagram, or adding the verbal principle, raised spontaneous access sharply. Reversing the arrows removed the benefit.
numbers: Exp 1: no-source baseline about 13%; both diagram groups equal to control before the hint; over 60% solved after the hint. Exp 2: control 11%; dynamic convergence 55% before hint, higher than static (which was at baseline), G2(1)=7.36, p<.01; divergence versions no better than control. Exp 3 (N=20 per cell): static+principle 45%, dynamic+principle 50% before hint; totals 70% vs 95%. Exp 4 (blocks not arrows, N=20 per cell): static 5% vs dynamic 30% before hint, G2=4.72, p<.05.
quote: Static diagrams ... were not accessed spontaneously but were often used successfully once a hint to consider the diagram had been provided.
limits: UCLA undergraduates; cells of 20; animation is perceptual and does not carry over to text.
agent_relevance: Encoding the source as a motion or force relation, plus stating the principle, makes it recognisable. The pre-hint vs post-hint gap shows noticing, not applying, is the bottleneck.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1980, 1983) baseline figures as restated in Pedone et al. (2001) and Gentner et al. (1993)
finding: The classic radiation-problem figures: about 10% solve with no source, about 30% with a verbal military source, about 75 to 80% total after a hint. Gick (1985) found a similar pre/post-hint gap with diagrams.
numbers: Control about 10%; verbal analogue about 30% spontaneous, about +50 points after hint, roughly 80% total (Pedone) or 75% (GRF93); Figure 1 diagrams: spontaneous equal to baseline 10%, about 70% after hint.
limits: Secondhand restatement; the 1980 and 1983 tables themselves were not opened (Michigan page returned 403). Other summaries quote 92% after hint.
agent_relevance: Use the shape (about 3x from a source, a further 2.5x from a hint), not a fixed percentage.

source: Holyoak and Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer (via slides in a search snippet)
finding: Spontaneous transfer from a lightbulb story to the radiation problem needed both surface and structural similarity. Lowering either cut spontaneous use. After a hint, structure mattered for success.
numbers: Before hint: fragile-glass/laser 69%, fragile-glass/ultrasound 38%, insufficient-intensity/laser 33%, insufficient-intensity/ultrasound 13%. After hint: 75%, 81%, 60%, 47%.
limits: Numbers come from a search-result summary of a slide deck, not the paper; check Memory and Cognition 15:332-340. GRF93 says access was influenced about equally by surface and structural similarity.
agent_relevance: Both similarity types gate access. A representation that lowers surface distance and keeps constraint structure gives the best odds.

source: Holyoak and Koh (1987) and Keane, Ross, Reed lines of work, as reviewed in GRF93
finding: Review of rival accounts. Surface similarity matters most at access, structure at mapping. Keane argued people may have too little domain knowledge to judge structure, so preferring surface matches can be rational. Training can reduce the bias: Faries and Reiser's intensively trained subjects accessed structural matches despite competing surface similarity.
numbers: Holyoak and Koh: spontaneous access influenced about equally by surface and structural similarity; mapping success only by structure. Gick and Holyoak: about 10% baseline, about 30% with story, about 75% with a general hint.
limits: Review written by the structure-mapping side. The domain-knowledge rival is not ruled out by the evidence cited.
agent_relevance: Expertise and training reduce, but do not remove, the surface bias. Teach the agent's retrieval to expect that bias.

source: Catrambone and Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer (as cited in GRF93 and Gentner et al. 2009)
finding: As reported by Gentner and colleagues: people showed more relational retrieval when required to compare two prior analogs, but not when they only read both. Two downloads of the original PDF came back truncated, so the paper text was not read.
numbers: Not available from the original.
limits: Secondhand only. Consistent between the 1993 and 2009 papers.
agent_relevance: Reading two cases is not enough; the act of comparing is the active ingredient.

source: Kurtz and Loewenstein (2007) Converging on a new role for analogy in problem solving and retrieval: when two problems are better than one (search snippet)
finding: Comparing two unsolved target problems raised transfer from a studied source analogue compared with the standard condition; solving the two problems separately did not help, so comparison itself is active.
numbers: No numbers in the snippet; Gentner et al. (2009) Exp 5 extends it with a filled delay (tumor problem 31% vs 5%).
limits: Search snippet only; the Springer page was not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives a second trigger: when two similar current problems are open, compare them with each other before searching memory.

source: Trench and Minervino (2015) The role of surface similarity in analogical retrieval (search abstract)
finding: Two studies using a production paradigm (people generate their own analogs) found a strong effect of surface similarity on retrieval from their own memory. This answers Blanchette and Dunbar's claim that the surface bias is a lab artifact.
numbers: No numbers in the snippet.
limits: Abstract via search result only; not opened.
agent_relevance: The surface bias persists when people use their own memories, so do not expect it to vanish in realistic settings.

source: Trench (2014) Explaining the abundance of distant analogies in naturalistic observations of experts (commentary)
finding: Rival explanation for field studies that found many far analogies from experts: the generation task, not expertise, lets distant sources appear. Novices doing the same generation task also produce distant analogies, and experts did not differ from novices on a management task.
numbers: Blanchette and Dunbar (2000) replicated their journalist and politician result in novices; Trench et al. (2009) replicated across 10 target topics; Bearman et al. (2007) found no expert-novice difference. No new data in this commentary.
quote: The naturalistic observation of experts shows a more flexible use of analogical sources than is predicted by experimental studies on analogical transfer.
limits: Short commentary that reviews other studies and cites work I did not open. It states the retrieval mechanisms invariably favour close sources.
agent_relevance: Distant analogies are cheap to produce by generation and expensive to find by lookup. This is the same split the agent faces: generate (analogical prompting) vs look up (library).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Asking an LLM to recall three to five distinct relevant problems, then solve the original, beat zero-shot and chain-of-thought and matched or beat few-shot CoT with hand-written exemplars. Gains are small on strong models and large where the CoT baseline is weak.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, analogical 77.8; PaLM2 80.7 vs 81.7; text-davinci-003 0-shot CoT 50.3 vs 61.0. MATH: GPT-3.5 0-shot CoT 33.9 vs 37.3; PaLM2 34.3 vs 34.8. Codeforces GPT-3.5 Acc@1 9 (0-shot CoT) vs 13, with knowledge first 15; GPT-4 16 (CoT) vs 17 vs 19. BIG-Bench GPT-3.5: logical deduction 35.2 to 41.6, colored objects 61.6 to 68.0, word sorting 67.6 to 75.2, temporal 44.8 to 57.6 (3-shot CoT 58.0).
limits: Single runs, no confidence intervals; gaps over strong baselines are 0.5 to 3 points on GSM8K and MATH. GPT-3.5 and PaLM2 era models.
agent_relevance: Self-generated recall is a cheap, label-free exemplar source. The gain over a good plain CoT is small on strong models, so it is not a strong lever alone.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ablations)
finding: Diversity instruction, number of exemplars and model scale all matter. With small models, retrieved labelled exemplars beat self-generated ones; the lead flips at text-davinci-002/003. Self-consistency stacks on top.
numbers: Without a diversity instruction: GSM8K 75.9 vs 77.8, MATH 35.2 vs 37.3. K=1 GSM8K 76.1 / MATH 34.8; K=3 77.5 / 37.3; K=5 77.8 / 37.1. GSM8K by model (0-shot CoT / 5-shot retrieved CoT / ours): curie-001 2/3/2, davinci-001 6/11/9, davinci-002 22/47/48, davinci-003 50/57/61. With self-consistency: GSM8K 77.8 to 85.3, MATH 37.3 to 46.0. Error audit of 50 failures: 10 irrelevant exemplars, 12 relevant but wrong, 28 relevant and correct but the model still failed.
limits: Authors' own ablations, mostly one model. Knowledge-before-exemplars on Codeforces GPT-3.5 only 14 vs 15 Acc@1 and 27 vs 29 Acc@10.
agent_relevance: Ask for several varied analogues, not one. The main failure is a generalisation gap from an easier analogue to a harder target, not retrieval. Use only with strong models.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: A direct test of whether relevance drives the gain in analogical prompting. On math, self-generated irrelevant or random examples did as well or better than relevant ones; on BIG-Bench Hard relevant examples were best on average. The accuracy of the generated examples, not their relevance, was the key factor.
numbers: GPT-3.5 (temperature 0, seeds averaged): relevant 71.5 GSM8K / 33.3 MATH / 52.4 average; no relevance instruction (N/A) 75.5 / 36.1 / 55.8; random same-type 75.1 / 36.3; random different-type 76.3 / 34.1; random biology 75.3 / 34.6 (about 2.5 points over relevant on average). BBH: relevant beat N/A by 1.3 points on average. Pilot of 50 samples per type: relevant generated problems were harder and less often correct. Extra models: GPT-4o-mini, Llama, Qwen 2.5; extra task GPQA.
quote: The key factor is the accuracy of self-generated examples.
limits: Reversal shows on math only; BBH tasks support relevance. Differences are 1 to 4 points. I did not read the N/A prompt wording in detail.
agent_relevance: Direct counter-evidence to the relevance story. Check self-recalled examples by running them rather than trusting that they are analogous, in line with G2 and G3.

source: Li et al. (2025) Past meets present: creating historical analogy with large language models
finding: For finding historical events analogous to a given event, free generation by the LLM beat retrieval from a fixed event pool (embedding cosine, with or without LLM rerank of top 10). Self-reflection added more. Results are better on popular analogies, which suggests training-data leakage.
numbers: Free generation beat dataset retrieval by an average of 0.25 in Pass@1 (scale 0 to 1); Llama3.1-8B and gpt-3.5-turbo-0125; retrieval used text-embedding-3-small cosine.
limits: The pool (Google Arts and Culture) is small, so retrieval is limited by coverage as well as ranking; some metrics are LLM-assisted.
agent_relevance: If the library has no good case, generation from the model's own knowledge covers more ground than lookup. A library helps only when it contains the analogue.

source: Sultan, Stern, Shahaf (2025) Reliable proof generation with LLMs via analogical retrieval and symbolic verification
finding: In SAT-level geometry, retrieving structurally analogous solved problems (a small learned similarity predictor on abstracted problem features) raised proof accuracy with the same verifier and budget. A size-matched random set helped much less.
numbers: Same budget (3 runs x 5 retries): o1 52 to 80, Gemini-Flash-2.5 72 to 86, Claude Sonnet 4.6 78 to 86, GPT-5 88 to 96. First run, no retries: o1 10 to 48, Gemini 22 to 48, Claude 28 to 60, GPT-5 44 to 64. Ablation (apparently Gemini first run): size-matched random analogies 32% vs 48% analogy-derived vs 22% baseline. Predictor: of pairs scored above 0.95 (1.28% of pairs), 71% truly had high proof similarity. Top-100 analogous problems cover 96% of needed theorems with 26.66 theorems (13.6% of dictionary).
limits: 50 problems; one domain with a formal verifier; the ablation rows are read from garbled table text; the effect combines retrieval and verifier feedback.
agent_relevance: Best positive evidence for retrieval by an abstracted structural representation, paired with an executable check. Fits our plan: a verifier decides, retrieval only suggests.

source: Learning by analogy: enhancing few-shot prompting for math word problem solving with computational graph-based retrieval (2024)
finding: Training a retriever to pick exemplars whose computation graph is similar, rather than whose text embedding is similar, improved few-shot accuracy, most for small generators. The exception was math_qa, where surface and structure already coincide.
numbers: Average exact match over six datasets (random / BGE embedding / ours): Qwen-0.5B 18.6 / 27.6 / 34.3; 1.5B 27.6 / 40.7 / 47.1; 3B 52.7 / 57.6 / 60.8; 7-8B 59.7 / 66.2 / 68.8; 70-72B 66.3 / 72.8 / 74.4. Math23k Qwen-1.5B: ours 66.6, BGE 58.7, oracle graph retrieval 68.2. Gain with 10% of labels (about 2,000) still 4 points over BGE.
limits: Needs labelled computation graphs for training, or labels distilled from GPT-4o; gains shrink with model size (about 1.6 points at 70B).
agent_relevance: Retrieval by structure needs a structural representation. Gains are biggest for weak solvers. Where text similarity already tracks structure, embeddings are enough.

source: Rashid and Kellis (2026) Retrieved but not ranked: surface-form bias in structural retrieval
finding: Embedding retrieval anchors on wording. In math, with problems paraphrased so structure is kept but vocabulary changes, the right item is nearly always in the top 10 yet almost never first, because a planted lexical near-miss wins. In agent trajectories, retrieval is at or below chance once gold must use a different object.
numbers: Math (500 queries, 117,088 items): strict Hit@1 on the hard tier 0.0% [0.0, 0.0] for both production embedders; easy tier 12.2% Hit@1, 89.8% Hit@5, 97.6% Hit@10 (published 11.36 / 90.68 / 96.93); in 95.2 to 99.8% of misses the winner is more lexically similar to the query. Trajectories (118 queries, 336 items): Hit@1 17.8% (Qwen emb), 15.3% (Gemini emb), 9.3% (MiniLM) vs chance 15.3% under the different-object gold; below chance when object and receptacle both differ.
limits: Preprint dated Sep 2026, not peer reviewed; disguised queries were written by a Gemini-family model; the benchmark is built to make surface and structure disagree.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement of the human surface bias reappearing in embeddings. The agent must not rely on cosine similarity to find the analogous case. At minimum retrieve wide (top 10) and rerank by structure.

source: Rashid and Kellis (2026) Retrieved but not ranked: surface-form bias in structural retrieval (rerank, lexical control, downstream null)
finding: An LLM reranker over the top 10 recovers part of the gap, but size and even the best judge change with domain. A naive lexical reranker hurts on math and helps on trajectories. Reranking gains concentrate on famous competitions (memory). Downstream, giving the solver the gold analogous problem did not change accuracy.
numbers: Share of recoverable gap closed by judges in math from 5.4% to 63.3% depending on judge and tier. Lexical control on trajectories +25.9% [11.3, 41.2] (Qwen emb) and +36.4% [23.4, 50.0] (Gemini emb). Trajectory LLM rerank closes about 42 to 76%. Paired downstream test: 210 math queries, accuracy flat at 67 to 70% across no retrieval, adversarial top-1 and gold-with-solution (McNemar none vs gold: 13 hurt, 10 helped, p=.678); among the 127 queries finished within budget, accuracy 97.6 to 100% in all arms, so almost no headroom.
limits: Truncation artifacts in headline accuracy (authors list eight integrity incidents). Single solver (DeepSeek v4-flash). Part of the reranking gain may be memory of well-known problems.
agent_relevance: Perfect retrieval gave no accuracy gain where the solver already succeeded: retrieval only helps where the model fails. Measure headroom first, and do not trust one judge's rerank effect size.

source: Novick and Holyoak (1991) as cited in a 2026 arXiv paper (search snippet)
finding: Even with an explicit hint about which numbers correspond, successful transfer stayed low: only 50 to 68% succeeded. So access is one barrier and mapping or adaptation is a second.
numbers: 50 to 68% success when told exactly which numbers matched.
limits: Cited secondhand in a 2026 preprint seen only through search results; not opened.
agent_relevance: A retrieved analogue is not enough. The agent needs a separate mapping check (our O7) and must verify the transferred solution.
